title: Blog 1
content:
DOES SQS FIFO REALLY GUARANTEE “EXACTLY-ONCE PROCESSING”? An interesting scenario when studying asynchronous systems on AWS: an application receives the event “Order #1042 has been created”. AWS Lambda processes the message from Amazon SQS FIFO and writes to DynamoDB successfully, but the function times out just before deleting the message from SQS. The same message is received again afterward. Even when using a FIFO queue, why can duplicate processing still happen? This post clarifies the difference between duplicate-send prevention, order preservation, and preventing duplicate business effects, based on AWS Documentation.
Key points to remember:
Standard Queue delivers high throughput and at-least-once delivery, but messages may arrive more than once or out of order. FIFO Queue preserves ordering per MessageGroupId and provides message deduplication, while allowing different groups to be processed in parallel. SQS FIFO’s “exactly-once” applies to duplicate-send prevention at the messaging layer, not end-to-end execution of the entire business workflow inside Lambda. Deduplication has only a 5-minute window: resending the same MessageDeduplicationId within 5 minutes prevents another copy from entering the queue, whereas resending after 5 minutes may be treated as a new message. When content-based deduplication is enabled, SQS computes the deduplication ID using a SHA-256 hash of the message body only (excluding message attributes), so changing attributes alone does not create a distinct message for deduplication. Lambda + SQS event source mappings follow at-least-once semantics: if processing fails or times out, the message reappears after the visibility timeout and is processed again, even if the write already succeeded. Idempotency means running the same operation multiple times yields the same business outcome as running it once—for example, using DynamoDB PutItem with ConditionExpression: attribute_not_exists(eventId) to prevent overwriting an existing record. A conditional PutItem only protects that specific item write; if the workflow also sends emails, calls payment APIs, or updates external systems, you still need design patterns such as outbox/transactions, processing state tracking, or downstream idempotency keys. For batch retries, enable ReportBatchItemFailures to avoid retrying already-succeeded messages unnecessarily; on FIFO queues, stop at the first failure and include remaining unprocessed messages in batchItemFailures to preserve order. Configure a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount to route repeatedly failing messages to a FIFO Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ); DLQs help isolate and diagnose issues, though redriving later can break strict ordering and does not automatically fix logic errors. Review four core design questions for async systems: Is strict ordering required per group, and does MessageGroupId match the business entity (such as orderId)? Is reprocessing safe if a message reappears after the 5-minute window or due to a Lambda retry? Are visibility timeout, partial batch handling, and retry settings aligned with real-world processing duration? How will operators detect permanent failures, inspect payloads, and redrive messages from the DLQ? Conclusion: “Exactly-once delivery/deduplication” at the queue layer is not the same as “exactly-once business effect” at the application layer. Reliable event-driven workflows require combining FIFO ordering/deduplication, visibility timeout tuning, retry/DLQ handling, idempotency, and side-effect control. https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2344641672967458/

title: 5.1 · Problem and architecture
content:
An employee forwards a suspicious email while a colleague submits a screenshot of the same campaign. SecOps needs to preserve both originals, establish who can read each report and record the reason for a decision. This lab builds that process in US East (N. Virginia).
Open the full-resolution diagram · draw.io
How to read the diagram The browser loads React through CloudFront. Cognito issues a JWT. The HTTP API validates it for the Reporter and Admin APIs. The APIs use DynamoDB to check ownership, read incidents and record decisions. A browser uploads an image or EML directly to S3 using a presigned POST returned by the Reporter API. For pasted text or a demo fixture the Reporter API writes/copies the object. All three web paths produce uploads/{uuid}/raw. An S3 ObjectCreated notification calls Ingest. SES uses a separate receipt rule: store the original MIME in inbound/, then invoke Ingest with receipt verdicts. Ingest validates, computes SHA-256 and saves the raw object in the evidence bucket with versioning, SSE-KMS and seven-day Governance retention. After the save it starts the execution named for the incident, passing evidence references including raw_s3_key, raw_s3_version_id when available, and evidence_sha256. The sanitized bucket holds a separate redacted analysis copy. The SQS dead-letter queue receives failed async Ingest deliveries. Extract & Redact reads the evidence, runs Vietnamese/English Tesseract for images, and masks detectable PII. Insufficient usable text and QR evidence leads to NEEDS_MORE_INFO. Triage scores rules and checks indicators. Synthesize retrieves playbook passages and requests a Bedrock summary when configured. A deterministic fallback stays visible when synthesis fails. A high/critical report without a valid action goes to NEEDS_REVIEW with an SNS notice. A lower-risk report without a proposal ends at NO_ACTION. With a valid proposal, PrepareApproval persists the token and PENDING_APPROVAL before notifying SecOps. The Standard workflow holds the wait. The Lambda invocation returns. An admin reads the proposal and submits a decision. Admin API checks state and role, then calls SendTaskSuccess with the decision. Rejection ends at REJECTED. Expiry follows the timeout path to ESCALATED_TIMEOUT. An approval in the observed DRY_RUN mode records the simulated result and audit trail. Any blocklist entry is internal. External mail/firewall enforcement is outside this deployment. Two boundaries to point out. PhishGuardEdge protects traffic through CloudFront. The signed upload goes directly to S3. Lambda uses AWS-managed networking in this SAM template. The region and the service groups indicate placement and responsibility. QR extraction reads a URL locally, strips query and fragment for display, and supplies an indicator to Triage. The approval callback belongs to the Step Functions task that invokes PrepareApproval.

content:
Event Summary Report: “AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi 2026” Event Name: AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi 2026 Date & Time: 09:00 – 17:00, September 29, 2026 Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, District 1, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Role: Attendee Event Objectives Understand the transition of cloud computing, Generative AI, and Agentic AI from early experimentation to production-ready enterprise systems. Examine modern practices in cloud-native engineering, infrastructure automation, data platforms, workload identity, cloud security, and AI governance. Learn directly from Vietnamese enterprise customer stories on modernizing legacy architectures and operating reliably at scale. Analyze how security controls, governance frameworks, observability, and human oversight must adapt as AI systems gain autonomy. Map the technical insights from the event to my personal focus on cybersecurity and cloud security engineering. Speakers Dr. Werner Vogels – Chief Technology Officer, Amazon.com (Keynote Speaker) Eric Yeo – Country General Manager for Malaysia, Vietnam & Indochina, AWS Mai Le – Director of Product Management, Katalon Dr. Jens Lottner – Chief Executive Officer, Techcombank AWS Solutions Architects, Engineers, and Industry Leaders from Katalon, Techcombank, TCBS, Techcom Life, VPBank, and partner organizations Key Highlights Evolution from Cloud-Native Architecture to Agentic AI Moving beyond basic lift-and-shift migrations toward automated, self-healing, cloud-native architectures powered by containers, Kubernetes, serverless, event-driven patterns, and managed services. Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) establish standardized “Golden Paths” that eliminate repetitive infrastructure toil and TicketOps delays. Tools including Amazon EKS, Crossplane, Terragrunt, Backstage, FluxCD, and GitOps workflows ensure reproducible, consistent, auditable, and policy-controlled infrastructure delivery. Operationalizing Agentic AI in Production Building a functional AI agent prototype is straightforward compared to running it safely at enterprise scale, which rests on four foundational pillars: Operational Excellence: High availability, graceful failure recovery, latency budgets, and continuous monitoring. Data Governance: Clear data ownership, freshness, integrity, and granular access authorization. Security & Trust: Strict enforcement of workload identities, tool permissions, and sensitive data isolation. Human Oversight: Retaining human-in-the-loop approval for high-impact or irreversible operations. Technical deep dives on Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Strands Agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP), the ReAct reasoning loop, state persistence, and tool orchestration demonstrated how agents reason, retrieve context, invoke tools, and operate within explicit authorization guardrails. Workload Identity, Least Privilege, and AI Security Advancing past static, long-lived access keys toward cryptographically verifiable workload identities across trust boundaries. Core building blocks covered: AWS IAM, AWS STS (ephemeral credentials and short-lived sessions), trust policies, session policies and session tags, source identity, and Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) across EC2, ECS/Fargate, Lambda, EKS, CI/CD pipelines, multi-account environments, and AI agents. AI Governance, Data Provenance, and Trust Enterprise AI success hinges as much on data engineering and governance as on model selection—requiring data accuracy, freshness, lineage, ownership, access controls, grounded evidence, decision traceability, and safeguards against unsafe agent outputs. Summarized along the end-to-end security lifecycle: Identity → Data → Model → Tools → Agent → Action → Audit. Security Observability for AI Workloads Expanding traditional infrastructure telemetry (Four Golden Signals: Latency, Errors, Traffic, Saturation) with AI-specific observability pillars: Cost: Token consumption tracking and anomaly detection for runaway usage. Safety: PII leakage prevention, prompt injection detection, and unauthorized tool invocation blocking. Quality: Hallucination detection and output accuracy verification. Unifying infrastructure logs, IAM/identity events, data access trails, and AI agent behavioral telemetry. Secure AI-Assisted Software Development Kiro and AI-DLC embed AI across the entire Software Development Life Cycle—from architecture planning and code generation to automated testing, documentation, technical-debt reduction, and legacy modernization—highlighted by TCBS achieving a 26% reduction in development time. Emphasized pairing AI coding velocity with automated security checks, human code review, governance policies, and DevSecOps guardrails. Enterprise Cloud Modernization & Regulatory Compliance Real-world case studies from Techcombank, Techcom Life, TCBS, VPBank, and Katalon showcased application and database modernization, container adoption, unified data platforms, automated observability, and operational resilience. Highlighted AWS Local Zone in Hanoi and AWS Outposts (2nd Generation) for meeting strict Vietnamese data-residency and regulatory mandates while balancing Security, Compliance, Reliability, Performance, Cost, and Business Agility. Key Takeaways Security Engineering Mindset Identity as the primary perimeter: Every compute workload, CI/CD pipeline, microservice, and AI agent must operate with a distinct identity and ephemeral, least-privilege credentials. End-to-end AI security and human-in-the-loop controls: Safeguard the full execution chain (Identity → Data → Model → Tools → Agent → Action → Audit) and enforce human approval before high-risk actions execute. Holistic AI observability: Track agent reasoning, tool calls, data access, safety guardrails, output quality, and token spend alongside conventional system metrics. Cloud & Platform Architecture Declarative, auditable infrastructure: Favor managed services, containers, Kubernetes, serverless, GitOps, and IDPs over ad-hoc manual changes. Unified identity and data governance: Combine IAM, STS, workload identity, ABAC, cross-account boundaries, and curated data lineage. AI & Cybersecurity Convergence Verifiable safety over raw model capability: Validate that AI agents act strictly within authorized identities, permissions, and grounded data to mitigate emerging attack vectors (prompt injection, sensitive data exposure, privilege escalation, unauthorized tool execution, hallucinations, and cost spikes). Cross-disciplinary integration: Bridges Cloud Security, DevSecOps, AI Security, and Security Operations (SecOps). Application to My Work Enforce least-privilege IAM and short-lived sessions: Build hands-on labs practicing AWS IAM, STS role assumption, trust policies, ABAC, and cross-account access, verifying session tags in CloudTrail audit logs. Build unified cloud and AI security monitoring: Correlate infrastructure telemetry, identity logs, and AI agent activity, exploring how Wazuh and SIEM workflows extend into cloud-native and AI environments. Apply GitOps, IaC, and strict agent guardrails: Maintain version-controlled, auditable infrastructure and enforce explicit identity, permission, data-access, logging, and human-approval boundaries when building AI agents. Preserve human review in AI-assisted workflows: Leverage AI developer tools to accelerate delivery while maintaining rigorous security validation and human sign-off. Personal Experience & Reflection Attending the “AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi 2026” watch party and workshop offered a comprehensive look at how cloud-native platforms, agentic AI, and enterprise security converge in real production environments. Key highlights from my experience include:
Learning from Enterprise Leaders Sessions led by AWS executives and Vietnamese enterprise leaders (Techcombank, TCBS, VPBank, Techcom Life, and Katalon) demonstrated how large organizations balance rapid cloud and AI modernization with strict regulatory compliance, operational stability, and cultural transformation. Concrete production case studies bridged high-level architectural concepts with real-world operational constraints. Broad Technical Exposure Gained structured exposure to Amazon EKS, Kubernetes, GitOps, IAM, STS, Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore, MCP, AI-DLC, data governance, and AI security observability. Strengthened my understanding of workload identity, least-privilege enforcement, infrastructure-as-code automation, and monitoring AI safety, quality, and cost. Core Lessons Learned Scaling automation without strong governance amplifies security risks just as quickly as it boosts engineering velocity. Greater AI autonomy demands stricter identity boundaries, verifiable authorization, trusted data pipelines, and continuous lifecycle governance. Modern security engineers must be equipped not only to detect external threats, but also to architect, monitor, and govern AI systems safely. Event Photos Overall, the event delivered rich architectural and security insights that directly shaped my approach to cloud security, AI governance, observability, and building safe, human-supervised AI systems.

title: Blog 2
content:
AWS KMS & ENVELOPE ENCRYPTION: IS DATA ENCRYPTION ALREADY SECURE ENOUGH? An insightful question when studying AWS security: if an object in Amazon S3 is encrypted with AWS KMS (SSE-KMS), why can an authorized principal still download and read it normally? And a deeper question: why does enabling S3 Bucket Keys reduce requests to KMS while potentially breaking policies tied to an object ARN? Based on official AWS documentation, this post analyzes the underlying mechanics and security trade-offs rather than lab deployments or simulated results.
Key points to remember:
Envelope encryption uses two key layers: a symmetric data key encrypts the object payload, while a KMS key protects (encrypts) the data key. S3 requests a data key via GenerateDataKey, uses the plaintext data key briefly in memory to encrypt/decrypt data, and stores the encrypted data key with object metadata (while KMS Encrypt directly only supports small payloads up to 4,096 bytes for SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT). Encryption at rest does not replace authorization: reading an SSE-KMS object still requires valid S3 permissions plus kms:Decrypt (and uploading requires kms:GenerateDataKey), governed by IAM and KMS key policies. Compromised credentials with valid permissions can still read data through authorized APIs. Encryption context is a non-secret key-value map used as Additional Authenticated Data (AAD) and in policy conditions, and it can appear in plaintext in AWS CloudTrail—so never store secrets, passwords, or tokens in it. Without S3 Bucket Keys, S3 SSE-KMS includes the object ARN in the default encryption context (aws:s3:arn), enabling object-level policy conditions. S3 Bucket Keys can reduce KMS request costs by up to 99% using a time-bounded bucket-level key, but shift default aws:s3:arn in the encryption context from the object ARN to the bucket ARN and reduce per-object KMS CloudTrail events (without removing S3 access logs or bypassing S3 object permission checks). Cached bucket-level key operations do not trigger new KMS calls or re-evaluate the KMS key policy during those cached operations, and S3 Bucket Keys do not support DSSE-KMS. Four security review questions for KMS/S3 designs: (1) Are s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt scoped to least privilege? (2) Do policies enforce object-, prefix-, or bucket-level access and rely on specific encryption context keys? (3) Do KMS policy assumptions and CloudTrail granularity still hold if S3 Bucket Keys are enabled? (4) Are key management, credential protection, and activity monitoring designed together? Conclusion: Encryption is not a silver bullet against unauthorized use of valid credentials. AWS KMS adds value through key lifecycle management, access control, and auditability—meaning every cost or performance optimization must be reviewed for security control and traceability trade-offs. https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2342975263134099/

title: 2. Project proposal
content:
PhishGuard AI · Omnichannel phishing triage with human approval
Proposed pilot: an internal security operations team and employees reporting suspicious messages. Deployment region: US East (N. Virginia). The demo runs containment in DRY_RUN.
The operational problem An employee forwards a suspicious message to a general mailbox. A second employee reports an image of the same campaign. The analyst needs to identify each reporter, preserve precisely what each person submitted, explain a recommendation and find the decision later. Copying text into a chatbot helps with interpretation. Someone still has to connect the evidence, access controls, reviewer and outcome.
What the pilot delivers A Cognito-authenticated portal accepts pasted text, screenshots and EML files. An SES receiving rule accepts forwarded email from verified reporters. Ingest gives each report an incident ID and preserves a version of the original. Analysts use a redacted copy for routine work. A separate, audited request gives a privileged analyst short-lived access to the original.
The policy engine computes the score from indicators and named rules. Bedrock can retrieve playbooks and explain the result. If generation fails, the analyst still sees the rule result and the fallback reason. Where an action is proposed, Step Functions records a deadline, notifies SecOps and resumes only on a valid decision or a timeout. Approval records retain the human decision. A simulated block, a confirmed entry in the internal list and enforcement by an external product have different operational effects. External enforcement is outside the pilot.
Deliverables and acceptance Milestone Deliverable How to accept it Intake and preservation Portal, SES and separate evidence stores Submit a UTF-8 message and an image, then trace an incident to its S3 version. Repeating the same reporter request returns its incident. Analysis OCR, PII masking, policy evaluation and grounded summary Inspect the extracted Vietnamese text, triggered rules and evidence. Low-quality input asks for more information. Record the actual synthesis status. Approval Admin decision, callback and audit log An approved demo produces an audit record. An unanswered request expires. A late decision returns HTTP 409. Operations and handover Role-specific reads, alarms, workshop and cost model A second reporter cannot read the first reporter’s incident. Demonstrate alarm targets, a reproducible deployment and the assumptions behind cost. Boundaries and risks Object Lock Governance protects a raw version for seven days subject to authorized bypass. OCR may miss accents and masking can leave names or addresses. Forwarded headers describe the original message as supplied by the employee. SES authentication proves facts about the outer delivery. Analysts must interpret those separately. False-positive and false-negative rates on unseen real-world messages still require a labelled evaluation set.
Deployed scope. The CloudFront distribution has the PhishGuardEdge web ACL. Raw uploads go directly to S3. Image extraction supports Vietnamese/English OCR and URL QR codes. Five source playbooks support retrieval. Triage proposes eligible actions and Bedrock explains them.
Costs and pilot decision For a 30-day month with 300 reports, 90 images and 60 inbound emails, the model estimates USD 9.37, including the permanent WAF rules and one hosted zone. The Cost Explorer report for 1–23 November 2026 rounds to USD 0.00 within its export scope. Before extending the pilot, compare time to triage, false alerts, missed cases and manual review against the current mailbox process using an independently labelled set.

title: Blog 3
content:
HAS AMAZON S3 BLOCK PUBLIC ACCESS ALREADY MADE YOUR DATA SAFE? When learning AWS security, Amazon S3 Block Public Access is one of the first controls you encounter. Yet an important question arises: if a valid IAM access key with S3 read permissions is exposed, will Block Public Access stop unauthorized data access? Not necessarily—it primarily blocks public access granted via bucket policies or ACLs, not authorized calls made with leaked credentials or missing least-privilege controls. This post frames S3 data protection across three layers: Prevention, Auditing, and Detection & Alerting.
Key points to remember:
Prevention: Enable all four Block Public Access settings (BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets), where S3 applies the most restrictive combination across levels; remember that private buckets still allow principals with valid s3:GetObject permissions, so enforce least privilege. Note also that new buckets default to Bucket owner enforced (ACLs disabled) and default SSE-S3 encryption (since January 5, 2023), which protects data at rest without replacing access control. Auditing: Investigating unexpected reads or deletions requires object-level API logs (GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject) via AWS CloudTrail S3 Data Events, which are not enabled by default on trails—route logs to a dedicated audit bucket and scope tracked events/buckets to control cost. Detection & Alerting: GuardDuty S3 Protection analyzes S3 object-level API activity for anomalies such as Exfiltration:S3/AnomalousBehavior without requiring you to manually enable S3 Data Events on your CloudTrail trail; route findings via EventBridge to SNS (with confirmed email subscriptions and realistic filtering) and verify evidence before taking action. CLI & Safe Testing: Inspect settings read-only with aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket YOUR_BUCKET_NAME, test alert pipelines safely using GuardDuty Generate sample findings, and watch costs for CloudTrail data events and GuardDuty S3 Protection. Conclusion: Turning on Block Public Access is only a starting point. Combining Prevention, Auditing, and Detection & Alerting provides defense in depth so you can restrict access, trace actions, and spot anomalous behavior together. https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2341941026570856/

title: Blogs Posted
content:
This section lists and introduces the blogs posted to AWS Study Group, focusing on AWS security mechanics, least privilege, data protection, and incident response.
Blog 1 - DOES SQS FIFO REALLY GUARANTEE “EXACTLY-ONCE PROCESSING”? This blog clarifies why duplicate processing can still happen on Amazon SQS FIFO queues—such as when a Lambda function writes to DynamoDB and times out before deleting the message—by distinguishing queue-level deduplication (5-minute window, SHA-256 on message body only) from end-to-end business effects, while covering Lambda at-least-once retries, idempotency (ConditionExpression on PutItem), external side effects, ReportBatchItemFailures on FIFO queues, FIFO DLQ redrive trade-offs, and four core async design questions.
Blog 2 - AWS KMS & ENVELOPE ENCRYPTION: IS DATA ENCRYPTION ALREADY SECURE ENOUGH? This blog examines how S3 SSE-KMS uses envelope encryption (GenerateDataKey and data keys vs. KMS keys), why encryption at rest does not replace authorization, how encryption context works as non-secret AAD, and how S3 Bucket Keys reduce KMS request costs (up to 99%) while shifting default aws:s3:arn from object ARN to bucket ARN and affecting KMS policy evaluation and CloudTrail granularity.
Blog 3 - HAS AMAZON S3 BLOCK PUBLIC ACCESS ALREADY MADE YOUR DATA SAFE? title: Blog 4
content:
HOW CAN A SINGLE IAM PERMISSION CAUSE MAJOR RISKS? ANALYZING ADMINISTRATORACCESS ON AWS In AWS operations, access control is foundational to cloud security, and AWS IAM lets administrators manage user permissions across services and resources. However, granting overly broad permissions—especially AdministratorAccess—creates severe risks if credentials leak or an identity is compromised. What happens when an IAM identity with full administrative privileges is taken over? This post examines the key blast-radius risks across AWS services and practical controls to reduce them.
Key points to remember:
AdministratorAccess is an AWS Managed Policy granting near-full administrative control across the account; if compromised, attackers can exfiltrate or delete S3 data, launch unauthorized EC2 instances (such as for cryptojacking) or disrupt running workloads, modify/delete RDS instances or snapshots, create persistent IAM users/roles/access keys, and tamper with or disable CloudTrail logging. Reduce blast radius by enforcing least privilege instead of defaulting to AdministratorAccess, requiring MFA on privileged identities, and preferring temporary credentials via IAM roles over long-lived access keys. Use permission boundaries to cap maximum permissions an IAM user or role can obtain, monitor IAM and security configuration changes via AWS CloudTrail (with independent log protection), and conduct regular access reviews to revoke unused or overly broad permissions. https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2346868572744768/

title: Blog 5
content:
AWS ACCESS KEY EXPOSED ON GITHUB: AWS ALREADY QUARANTINED IT—WHAT ELSE MUST WE DO? When reading about exposed AWS access keys, it is easy to assume that automatic AWS detection and mitigation mean the risk is minor. In reality, AWS helps detect and limit impact, but automated quarantine does not mean the account is automatically safe or that incident response is finished. This post outlines what AWS does when an exposed key is detected, the five steps to respond, and ways to prevent exposure in personal and team projects.
Key points to remember:
What AWS Does Automatically: AWS can detect credentials exposed on sources such as GitHub, attach quarantine policies (such as AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3 or AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV4) to the IAM identity, and notify via AWS Health or a Support Case (with Unit 42 observing a ~10-second V3 policy attachment in one test, though response time is not guaranteed). Quarantine policies add explicit Deny statements on specific actions rather than disabling the key outright, so remaining allowed actions still depend on the identity’s other IAM permissions. 5-Step Incident Response: (1) Isolate the exposed key by identifying the IAM user, checking permissions, and setting the key to Inactive first rather than deleting immediately when operational correlation helps; (2) restore legitimate access by updating workloads and migrating from long-term keys to IAM roles/temporary credentials; (3) investigate activity in AWS CloudTrail (APIs, timestamps, source IPs, regions, and IAM/resource changes) using an independent admin principal and accounting for log scope such as S3 data events; (4) check for compromise across the wider account (new/modified IAM users, roles, policies, EC2/Lambda/S3 resources, unusual regions, and billing anomalies); and (5) close out remediation by following the AWS Support Case guidance rather than removing the quarantine policy prematurely just because workloads recover. Prevention First: Favor IAM roles for AWS workloads, IAM Identity Center/federation over long-term user keys, GitHub Actions OIDC instead of long-lived secrets, GitHub Secret Scanning with Push Protection, and local hooks like git-secrets—and remember that deleting a file or commit does not make a leaked secret safe once exposed. https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2346834029414889/

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Participating in the AWS First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program has been a rewarding milestone in my academic and technical journey. Below are my honest reflections and constructive feedback based on my 12-week experience building PhishGuard AI with my team:
Overall Evaluation 1. Working Environment
The learning and working environment at FCAJ—especially during sessions and weekly meetups at Bitexco Financial Tower—is energetic, welcoming, and collaborative. Fellow builders and program coordinators are always willing to share insights and troubleshoot issues even outside regular syncs. Adding a few informal cross-team networking or bonding sessions early in the cohort would make it even easier for interns from different groups to connect.
2. Support from Mentor / Team Admin
The mentors provided sharp, architecture-level feedback rather than handing out ready-made solutions. During our PhishGuard AI design reviews, mentor critiques helped us uncover critical edge cases—such as forwarded email DMARC validation, idempotency collisions, and compensating controls for direct S3 Presigned POST uploads—pushing us to think like production cloud security engineers. The admin team also maintained clear documentation templates, portals, and responsive logistical support throughout the program.
3. Relevance of Work to Academic Major
As an Information Security student, building a Human-in-the-Loop Phishing Triage & SOAR Copilot on AWS Serverless aligned directly with my major. It allowed me to apply core security principles—Least Privilege IAM, RBAC, cryptographic evidence integrity (S3 Object Lock & KMS), PII redaction, and AI Guardrails against Prompt Injection—to a practical, end-to-end cloud architecture.
4. Learning & Skill Development Opportunities
The program accelerated both my technical depth and engineering workflow. Beyond hands-on mastery of AWS SAM, Step Functions, Amazon Bedrock (RAG & Guardrails), Textract, and CloudFront/WAF, I learned how to write rigorous technical specifications, estimate cloud costs via AWS Pricing Calculator, design acceptance test suites, and collaborate effectively in a 5-member engineering team.
5. Community Culture & Team Spirit
FCAJ fosters a strong builder culture where knowledge sharing is genuine and constructive. Whether during Saturday meetups, architecture reviews, or late-sprint debugging with teammates, everyone supported one another with mutual respect and shared enthusiasm for Cloud and AI.
6. Program Resources & Benefits
The $200 AWS Credits lab roadmap gave us a structured, low-risk way to get hands-on with core services before architecting our capstone project. Additionally, complimentary access to flagship community events—such as AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi 2026, Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels, Buildrathon Kickoff, and FCAJ Weekly Meetups—was an invaluable highlight of the program.
Additional Questions What did you find most satisfying during your internship?
Seeing PhishGuard AI evolve from an initial whiteboard idea into a live, end-to-end serverless security platform where deterministic rules, PII redaction, Bedrock RAG/Guardrails, and human-in-the-loop Step Functions approvals worked seamlessly together—and validating that our risk scoring remained invariant even against real Prompt Injection payloads.
What do you think the program should improve for future interns?
Providing a dedicated sandbox environment or pre-verified test domain guidelines earlier in the program would help teams testing email-driven services (such as Amazon SES Inbound) avoid DNS propagation bottlenecks and account sandbox limits.
If recommending to a friend, would you suggest they intern here? Why or why not?
Definitely yes. FCAJ bridges the gap between university theory and real-world AWS cloud engineering. You are challenged to design, cost-optimize, secure, and deploy a complete production-style system from scratch while learning directly from experienced AWS practitioners and community leaders.
Suggestions & Expectations Do you have any suggestions to improve the internship experience?
Hosting a mid-program “Architecture & Security Clinic” where teams can do quick 15-minute peer reviews of each other’s IAM policies, cost estimates, and edge cases before the final MVP sprint would add great value.
Would you like to continue this program in the future?
Yes, I would love to stay involved with the FCAJ community—both to deepen my specialization in Cloud Security & AI Security and to return in future cohorts as a supporter or mentor for incoming students.
Any other comments (free sharing):
Thank you to the entire FCAJ organizing team, mentors, guest speakers, and my four teammates for an unforgettable 12-week journey. The engineering habits, security mindset, and community connections I gained here will stay with me throughout my career.
